---
title: "Bayesian linear regression"
execute:
  enabled: true

The Provo Gaussian linear model can be combined with a prior to produce a posterior distribution over regression lines. Recall from [posterior distributions](../statistical-inference/posterior-distributions.qmd) that updating multiplies a likelihood by a prior and then normalizes the product. The response model remains the Gaussian specification stated below.

The derivation has three parts: we first specify a conjugate prior, then update its parameters from the likelihood, and finally compute posterior summaries and fitted means.

$$
\mathbf Y\mid\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2
\sim
\mathcal N(\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2\mathbf I).
$$

What changes is that uncertainty about $\boldsymbol\beta$ and $\sigma^2$ is represented before and after observing the responses.

## A conjugate prior specification

We use the normal--inverse-gamma specification

$$
\boldsymbol\beta\mid\sigma^2
\sim
\mathcal N(\mathbf b_0,\sigma^2\mathbf V_0)
$$

and

$$
\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InverseGamma}(a_0,d_0).
$$

We use the shape--scale parameterization

$$
p(\sigma^2)
\propto
(\sigma^2)^{-(a_0+1)}
\exp\left(-\frac{d_0}{\sigma^2}\right),
$$

whose mean is $d_0/(a_0-1)$ when $a_0>1$. Conditional conjugacy is useful here because it makes every updating step visible. It is not a claim that a normal--inverse-gamma prior is required for regression.

## From likelihood and prior to posterior

The likelihood kernel is

$$
p(\mathbf y\mid\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2)
\propto
(\sigma^2)^{-n/2}
\exp\left[
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)^\top
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)
\right].
$$

Multiplying by the conditional normal prior adds the quadratic

$$
(\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf b_0)^\top
\mathbf V_0^{-1}
(\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf b_0).
$$

Collect the terms involving $\boldsymbol\beta$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\boldsymbol\beta^\top
(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X+\mathbf V_0^{-1})
\boldsymbol\beta\\
&\quad-2\boldsymbol\beta^\top
(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf y+\mathbf V_0^{-1}\mathbf b_0)
+\mathbf y^\top\mathbf y
+\mathbf b_0^\top\mathbf V_0^{-1}\mathbf b_0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Define

$$
\mathbf V_n^{-1}=\mathbf V_0^{-1}+\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X,
\qquad
\mathbf V_n^{-1}\mathbf b_n
=\mathbf V_0^{-1}\mathbf b_0+\mathbf X^\top\mathbf y.
$$

Completing the square yields

$$
(\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf b_n)^\top
\mathbf V_n^{-1}
(\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf b_n)
+
\mathbf y^\top\mathbf y
+\mathbf b_0^\top\mathbf V_0^{-1}\mathbf b_0
-\mathbf b_n^\top\mathbf V_n^{-1}\mathbf b_n.
$$

The first term is the kernel of the updated conditional normal distribution. The remaining scalar joins the inverse-gamma scale. Thus the posterior parameters are the quantities left by completing the square.

The posterior is again normal--inverse-gamma, with

$$
\mathbf V_n
=
(\mathbf V_0^{-1}+\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1},
$$

$$
\mathbf b_n
=
\mathbf V_n
(\mathbf V_0^{-1}\mathbf b_0+\mathbf X^\top\mathbf y),
$$

$$
a_n=a_0+\frac n2,
$$

and

$$
d_n
=
d_0+\frac12
\left(
\mathbf y^\top\mathbf y
+\mathbf b_0^\top\mathbf V_0^{-1}\mathbf b_0
-\mathbf b_n^\top\mathbf V_n^{-1}\mathbf b_n
\right).
$$

## Computing the posterior

```{r}
#| label: fit-provo-bayesian-regression
library(ggplot2)

provo <- read.csv(
  "data/provo/content-word-positions.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
provo$cloze_surprisal_bits <- -log2(provo$OrthoMatchModel)
provo$cloze_surprisal_c <-
  provo$cloze_surprisal_bits - mean(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits)

ols_fit <- lm(mean_log_ffd ~ cloze_surprisal_c, data = provo)
X <- model.matrix(ols_fit)
y <- provo$mean_log_ffd
residual_scale <- summary(ols_fit)$sigma

b0 <- c(mean(y), 0)
V0 <- diag(c(
  (2 * sd(y) / residual_scale)^2,
  (2 * sd(y) / (sd(provo$cloze_surprisal_c) * residual_scale))^2
))
a0 <- ncol(X) + 1
d0 <- (a0 - 1) * residual_scale^2

Vn <- solve(solve(V0) + crossprod(X))
bn <- drop(Vn %*% (solve(V0) %*% b0 + crossprod(X, y)))
an <- a0 + nrow(provo) / 2
dn <- as.numeric(
  d0 + .5 * (
    crossprod(y) +
      t(b0) %*% solve(V0) %*% b0 -
      t(bn) %*% solve(Vn) %*% bn
  )
)

set.seed(20261019)
n_draws <- 4000L
sigma2_draws <- 1 / rgamma(n_draws, shape = an, rate = dn)
beta_noise <- matrix(
  rnorm(n_draws * ncol(X)),
  nrow = n_draws
) %*% chol(Vn)
beta_draws <- matrix(
  bn,
  nrow = n_draws,
  ncol = ncol(X),
  byrow = TRUE
) + sweep(beta_noise, 1, sqrt(sigma2_draws), `*`)
colnames(beta_draws) <- colnames(X)

slope_interval <- quantile(
  beta_draws[, "cloze_surprisal_c"],
  c(.025, .975)
)

stopifnot(
  all(is.finite(beta_draws)),
  all(is.finite(sigma2_draws)),
  slope_interval[[1]] < slope_interval[[2]]
)

data.frame(
  posterior_mean_slope = mean(beta_draws[, "cloze_surprisal_c"]),
  posterior_sd_slope = sd(beta_draws[, "cloze_surprisal_c"]),
  lower = slope_interval[[1]],
  upper = slope_interval[[2]]
)
```

The code mirrors the algebra: `Vn` inverts prior precision plus data precision; `bn` multiplies that covariance by the prior-and-data information vector; `an` adds $n/2$; and `dn` is the constant left after completing the square. Because $1/\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a_n,d_n)$ under this parameterization, `1 / rgamma(..., rate = dn)` generates inverse-gamma draws. Conditional beta draws then add a Cholesky-transformed standard-normal vector scaled by each sampled $\sigma$.

The 4,000 draws are a Monte Carlo setting, not an inferential assumption. For a posterior mean, simulation error is approximately the posterior draw SD divided by $\sqrt{4000}$ because these conjugate draws are independent. More draws reduce numerical error but do not change the posterior distribution.

The posterior mean slope is `r sprintf("%.6f", mean(beta_draws[, "cloze_surprisal_c"]))`, with a central interval from `r sprintf("%.6f", slope_interval[[1]])` to `r sprintf("%.6f", slope_interval[[2]])`.

The coefficient-prior location and scale use the observed Provo response and predictor scales. The inverse-gamma shape is one plus the observed design dimension, and its scale sets the prior mean of $\sigma^2$ to the OLS residual variance. These data-dependent priors are useful for connecting conjugate algebra to regression, but they are not independently specified confirmatory priors.

The following prior-predictive calculation makes that limitation visible. It draws parameters from the data-calibrated prior and a response at centered surprisal before conditioning on the likelihood.

```{r}
#| label: check-provo-prior-predictive
set.seed(20261018)
n_prior_draws <- 1000L
prior_sigma2 <- 1 / rgamma(n_prior_draws, shape = a0, rate = d0) # dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
prior_beta_noise <- matrix(
  rnorm(n_prior_draws * ncol(X)),
  nrow = n_prior_draws
) %*% chol(V0)
prior_beta <- matrix(
  b0,
  nrow = n_prior_draws,
  ncol = ncol(X),
  byrow = TRUE
) + sweep(prior_beta_noise, 1L, sqrt(prior_sigma2), `*`)
colnames(prior_beta) <- colnames(X)
prior_mean_at_center <- prior_beta[, "(Intercept)"]
prior_response_at_center <- prior_mean_at_center +
  rnorm(n_prior_draws, sd = sqrt(prior_sigma2))

data.frame(
  quantity = c("mean at centered surprisal", "new response at centered surprisal"),
  lower = c(
    quantile(prior_mean_at_center, .025),
    quantile(prior_response_at_center, .025)
  ),
  median = c(
    median(prior_mean_at_center),
    median(prior_response_at_center)
  ),
  upper = c(
    quantile(prior_mean_at_center, .975),
    quantile(prior_response_at_center, .975)
  )
)
```

A [prior-predictive check](../statistical-inference/prior-predictive-distributions.qmd) ordinarily precedes looking at the responses. Here it documents the implications of a teaching prior already calibrated to those responses; it cannot retroactively make the prior independent of the sample.

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-bayesian-regression
#| fig-cap: "Provo positions with the posterior mean line and a central posterior interval for the conditional mean."
grid <- data.frame(
  cloze_surprisal_bits = seq(
    min(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits),
    max(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits),
    length.out = 160L
  )
)
grid$cloze_surprisal_c <-
  grid$cloze_surprisal_bits - mean(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits)
mu_draws <- outer(
  beta_draws[, "cloze_surprisal_c"],
  grid$cloze_surprisal_c,
  `*`
)
mu_draws <- sweep(mu_draws, 1, beta_draws[, "(Intercept)"], `+`)
grid$posterior_mean <- colMeans(mu_draws)
grid$lower <- apply(mu_draws, 2, quantile, probs = .025)
grid$upper <- apply(mu_draws, 2, quantile, probs = .975)

point_opacity <- 0.2
interval_opacity <- 0.2
ggplot(provo, aes(cloze_surprisal_bits, mean_log_ffd)) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = grid,
    aes(x = cloze_surprisal_bits, ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    fill = "#2C6E9B",
    alpha = interval_opacity
  ) +
  geom_point(color = "grey65", alpha = point_opacity, size = 0.8) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid,
    aes(y = posterior_mean),
    color = "#2C6E9B",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Modeled cloze surprisal (bits)",
    y = "Mean log first-fixation duration"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The posterior represents uncertainty under the same aggregated position likelihood. Bayesian updating does not restore participant observations or make the association causal.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Which part of the model is shared with OLS?
2. Why is this not a confirmatory prior analysis?
3. Why are predictions computed for every posterior draw?
4. Which data limitation survives the Bayesian formulation?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The Gaussian linear response model, including the straight conditional mean and common independent residual variance, is shared with OLS. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The coefficient and variance priors are calibrated from the observed predictor, response, and OLS residual scales rather than specified independently before seeing the data. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Evaluating the fitted mean within every joint draw propagates posterior covariance among coefficients into uncertainty about the prediction. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The data still contain reader-aggregated position summaries, so participant-level responses and dependence remain unavailable. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
